title: Kali: The Mother Beyond Fear
summary: A devotional month with Kali as her devotees know her: the Divine Mother of Bengal, sung to by Ramprasad and loved by Ramakrishna. Learn her names and image, her place in the Devi Mahatmya and Shakta devotion, how Kali Puja is kept, and how to offer red hibiscus, a lamp and song at a simple home puja, then decide whether to make a personal vow of devotion.
welcome:
This journey spends about a lunar month learning about Kali and offering her simple devotion (bhakti) at home. It is written for people who want to know her as she is actually worshipped: as Ma, the Mother, by millions of Hindus in Bengal, Assam, Odisha, Kerala, Nepal and across the diaspora, in great temples such as Kalighat and Dakshineswar and in family shrines, with songs, flowers and lamps.

You will learn her names and her image as her devotees read it, her story in the Devi Mahatmya, the Shakta poets and saints who loved her, how Kali Puja is kept, and how to make a small home puja with red hibiscus, a lamp and a sweet. For seven nights, ending on the new moon, you will sit with one aspect of the Mother each night and listen to the songs her devotees sing. At the end you may make a personal vow of devotion, or not.

Please read this plainly. This is not an initiation. Formal initiation (dīkṣā), tantric rites and the mantras a guru gives are not offered here and cannot be given by an app. Nothing here is "magic", a curse, a spell or "shadow work"; it is devotion. The best thing this journey can do is send you to a temple, a Kali Puja or a Hindu friend's home, to learn from the people whose religion this is.
about: Kali (Kālī, "the black one" and "she who is time", from kāla, which means both) is the Hindu Divine Mother in her fierce form. In the Devi Mahatmya she springs from the brow of the Goddess to destroy the demons Chanda and Munda, and drinks the blood of Raktabija so that no new demon can rise from it. In Tantric traditions she is the first of the ten Mahavidyas, the great wisdom goddesses, and for the Shakta tradition of Bengal she is the supreme reality itself. She is pictured dark blue or black, with wild hair, a garland of heads and a skirt of arms, holding a sword and a severed head in two hands and making the gestures of "do not fear" and of giving with the other two, her tongue out, standing on Shiva. Her devotees read every part of that image as the Mother's love: she cuts away ignorance and ego, ends what binds her children, and grants fearlessness and freedom. The eighteenth-century poet Ramprasad Sen sang to her as a child sings to its mother, and the nineteenth-century saint Ramakrishna, a priest at her temple at Dakshineswar near Kolkata, spent his life in her love. She is worshipped above all at Kali Puja, on the new-moon night of Diwali, and on new-moon nights through the year.
notes: Hinduism is a living religion. Kali belongs first to the Hindu families, temples and teachers who worship her, above all in the Shakta traditions. This journey is a respectful introduction and an invitation to learn from them, not a replacement.

Dīkṣā (formal initiation), tantric rites and mantras traditionally given by a guru are not offered here, and this journey does not describe or imitate them. Where Hindu prayers are mentioned, the app gives its own English words. Learn Sanskrit prayers, and their pronunciation and proper use, from a priest, teacher or family.

This is devotion, not magic. Kali is not a "dark goddess" of revenge, rage or shadow aesthetics, and she is not a weapon. Please do not use her, her image or her names in spells, curses or hexes, or treat her image as a dark aesthetic. Her devotees know her as the most loving of mothers.

Some temples, including some in Bengal, Assam and Nepal, have offered animal sacrifice (bali) to Kali, and a few still do; many Hindus oppose it, and many pujas offer a pumpkin, ash gourd or sugarcane instead. Some Bengali families also offer fish. This journey uses only vegetarian offerings, which are accepted everywhere.

Treat her image with care: keep it raised, clean and out of bathrooms; do not put it on shoes, floor mats, clothing as a design, or anything you sit on. Her image on T-shirts, tattoos and album covers has caused real offence.

The app can show the Hindu lunar calendar (panchang): tick it under "Also show" in "Calendar & holidays". It marks Amavasya and Diwali. Kali Puja in Bengal is kept on the same new moon, at night, and in some years a day apart; check a Bengali panchang or your local temple. Panchangs, regions and countries can differ by a day.

Safety: some sindoor and kumkum powders have been found to contain lead; buy lead-free and keep them from children. Night-time lamps and incense need a heatproof plate and constant attention. If sitting with fear brings up more than you can hold, stop, and talk to someone you trust or a professional; devotion is not a replacement for care.

stages.title: Coming to the Mother
stages.intro: Begin by learning who Kali is to her devotees, set up a small clean shrine, and offer a first simple puja: a lamp, a red hibiscus or other red flower, a sweet, and a few words to her as Mother.

lessons.title: Ma Kali
lessons.summary: Her names, her image as her devotees read it, and why they call her Mother.

sections.heading: Her names
sections.body:
Kālī is the feminine of kāla, a word that means both "black" and "time". She is the dark one, and she is time itself, which carries everything away. Her devotees in Bengal mostly call her simply Ma, "Mother", or Shyama, "the dark one", and her worship is often called Shyama Puja.

She has many other names. Kalika means the same as Kali. Dakshina Kali, "the gracious" or "the southward-facing" Kali, is the form most worshipped in Bengali homes and temples. Bhavatarini, "she who carries across the ocean of becoming", is her name at Dakshineswar. Adya Shakti is "the primal power". In Kerala she is Bhadrakali, "the auspicious Kali". Chamunda is the name the Devi Mahatmya gives her after her victory over Chanda and Munda.

sections.heading: Reading her image
sections.body:
Kali's image is startling at first. She is dark blue or black, naked or clad only in a skirt of severed arms, with wild loose hair, three eyes, and a garland of heads. Her tongue is out. In her four hands she holds a sword and a severed head, and makes two gestures: "do not fear" (abhaya) and the gesture of giving (varada). She stands on Shiva, who lies calm beneath her feet.

Her devotees read each detail as an image of grace. The sword cuts through ignorance; the severed head is the ego she has cut away; the garland, often of fifty heads, is said to be the letters of the Sanskrit alphabet, all sound and speech; the arms are the deeds, and their results, that she frees her devotees from. Her nakedness is freedom from every covering of illusion. And she gives with one hand and says "do not fear" with another: the terrible form is there to protect her children.

sections.heading: Kali and Shiva
sections.body:
Why does she stand on Shiva? A popular Bengali story says that after a battle she was dancing wildly, and the world was in danger, so Shiva lay down in her path. When she stepped on him she came to herself, and put out her tongue in shame. Many devotees and teachers give a deeper reading: Shiva is pure consciousness, still and silent, and Kali is its power (shakti), the energy that moves and acts. Without Shakti, Shiva is shava, a corpse; together they are the whole of reality. The pun on shiva and shava is old and loved.

Both readings are told today, and both are part of the tradition. Neither is a story of a goddess humiliating a god.

sections.heading: Starting in the right place
sections.body:
In the West Kali is often met first as a "dark goddess": a symbol of female rage, of destruction, of a shadow side to be explored. That picture comes mostly from colonial writers, horror films and modern Western spirituality, not from the people who worship her. For her devotees she is Ma, tender and fierce at once, the mother who frightens away whatever threatens her child.

That should shape how you come to her: learn first, ask before you join in, and treat her image as you would treat something holy of your own. Bengali communities are often warm toward respectful newcomers, and Kali Puja is a festival of lights, music and crowds. If you can, go and see one.

knowAndDont.known: Her names, her Dakshina Kali iconography, the devotional readings of her sword, garland and gestures, the Shakta understanding of Shiva as consciousness and Kali as its power, and her worship as Ma in Bengal are standard in living practice and in Shakta texts and poetry.
knowAndDont.unknown: The story of her tongue and her step on Shiva is popular and probably late; some scholars think the tongue was first a sign of her drinking Raktabija’s blood. The reading of the garland as the alphabet comes from Tantric texts whose dates are uncertain. How a fierce goddess of the battlefield became the tender Mother of Bengal is traced through many centuries.

lessons.inPractice: Find an image of Kali you can treat with care: a framed print of Dakshina Kali or of the Bhavatarini image at Dakshineswar, or a small murti (sacred image) from a Hindu shop or temple store. Learn to say her name: KAA-lee, with a long first a. Find out whether there is a Kali temple, or a Bengali community that keeps Kali Puja, near you.
reflect: What would it mean to you that the most frightening image of the Goddess is also the most loving?
What do you already assume about Kali that you might need to unlearn?
further: David Kinsley, Hindu Goddesses: Visions of the Divine Feminine in the Hindu Religious Tradition (1986), ch. 8
Rachel Fell McDermott and Jeffrey J. Kripal, eds., Encountering Kālī: In the Margins, at the Center, in the West (2003)

practices.title: Set up a small, clean shrine
practices.instructions:
Choose a raised place: a shelf or small table, never the floor, and never a bathroom. Many families keep the shrine in the north-east of the home; do this if you can. Clean it and lay a fresh red cloth.

Set her image at the back, at or above eye level when you sit. In front, place a small diya (oil lamp) with ghee or mustard oil on a heatproof plate, an incense holder, a dish for flowers, a small plate for sweets and a cup of clean water. A small bell is customary to ring as you begin. Keep a little lead-free sindoor or kumkum (red powder) if you like.

Keep it simple and keep it clean. Remove old flowers each day. Take your shoes off before you approach it.
practices.prompt: Where did you place her shrine, and how did you feel sitting before her image for the first time?

rite.title: First Flower for the Mother
rite.summary: A first short puja: wash, honour Ganesha, light the lamp, offer a red flower, water and a sweet, call her Ma in your own words, and sit quietly.

ingredients.name: A diya (small oil lamp) with ghee or mustard oil and a cotton wick, on a heatproof plate
One fresh red hibiscus, or another red flower such as a red rose
A small sweet, such as a sandesh or a piece of jaggery

rite.preparation: Bathe or wash your hands, feet and face, and put on clean clothes. Remove your shoes. Clean the shrine. Do not eat meat or drink alcohol beforehand. Unwrap the sweet without tasting it. Sit on a mat or cushion before the image.

steps.title: Settle
steps.instructions: Sit quietly before her. Join your palms at your chest and take a few slow breaths.

steps.title: Ganesha first
steps.instructions: Ring the bell gently. Many Hindus honour Ganesha first at the start of any puja. Bow to him in your mind, or before his image if you have one.
steps.spoken: Ganesha, remover of obstacles, I bow to you first.

steps.title: Light the lamp
steps.instructions: Light the diya, then the incense.

steps.title: Offer
steps.instructions: Offer water by holding the cup up a little and setting it down. Take the red flower in both hands, hold it to your heart for a moment, and place it at her feet. Then set the sweet before her. Flowers are offered whole and unsmelled; food is offered untasted.
steps.spoken:
Ma Kali, Mother, I bow to you.
I have come to learn who you are.
Accept this water, this flower and this sweet.

steps.title: Call her Ma
steps.instructions: Speak to her simply, as a child speaks to its mother: who you are, why you have come, and what you are afraid of, if you wish.

steps.title: Sit
steps.instructions: Look at her face in the lamplight, and at the hand that says "do not fear". Then close your eyes for a few minutes.

steps.title: Close
steps.instructions: Bow with joined palms. Let the lamp burn while you are present, then put it out gently by covering it or pinching it with a flower rather than blowing it out. Take the sweet as prasad.
steps.spoken: Thank you, Ma. I will come again.

rite.closing: Eat the sweet, or share it: what has been offered comes back as prasad, her grace. Return the flower to a plant pot or garden when it wilts. Pour the water onto a plant. Write a few lines in your journal.
rite.safety: Set the diya and incense on a heatproof plate away from curtains, cloth and paper, and never leave them unattended. Keep flame, smoke and sweets away from pets and children.

stages.title: Battlefield, Burning Ground and Temple
stages.intro: Three lessons: Kali in the Devi Mahatmya and the old texts; the Shakta poets and saints of Bengal who knew her as Mother; and her temples and Kali Puja. Light the lamp and offer a red flower before you study each day.

lessons.title: From the Brow of the Goddess
lessons.summary: The tongues of fire, Kali in the Devi Mahatmya, the Mahavidyas, and the dark night of time.

sections.heading: Early traces
sections.body:
The name Kali appears early, but not yet as the great goddess. In the Mundaka Upanishad (1.2.4), Kali, "the black one", is the first of the seven flickering tongues of the sacrificial fire. In the Mahabharata a figure called Kalaratri, "the night of time", appears to warriors in a vision of the slaughter to come. Fierce, dark goddesses of the edges, of battle, forest and burning ground, were honoured in many places.

Over centuries these streams came together. By the time of the Devi Mahatmya, around the fifth or sixth century CE, Kali has a clear place in the story of the Great Goddess.

sections.heading: In the Devi Mahatmya
sections.body:
If you have taken the Durga journey you will remember the Devi Mahatmya, "Glory of the Goddess", part of the Markandeya Purana. In its third story the Goddess fights the armies of Shumbha and Nishumbha. When their generals Chanda and Munda come against her, her face grows dark with anger, and from her brow springs Kali: gaunt, dark, wearing a tiger skin and a garland of heads, armed with a sword and noose, filling the sky with her roar. She destroys the two generals, and the Goddess names her Chamunda (canto 87 in Pargiter's 1904 translation).

Then comes Raktabija, "blood-seed", from every drop of whose blood a new demon springs. The Goddess asks Kali to open her mouth wide and drink his blood before it touches the ground, and so he is defeated (canto 88). Kali here is the Goddess's own fierce power, sent out to do what nothing else can, and drawn back into her at the end.

sections.heading: The Mahavidyas and the Tantras
sections.body:
In later Tantric traditions, Kali becomes far more than a warrior. She is the first of the ten Mahavidyas, the "great wisdom" goddesses, who include Tara, Tripura Sundari, Bhuvaneshvari, Chinnamasta and others. Tantric texts such as the Kali Tantra and the Mahanirvana Tantra praise her as the supreme reality, beyond time, the one who swallows time itself. Her Tantric worship is learned only through initiation from a guru, within a lineage.

This is where much Western confusion comes from. Tantric rites were secret, and outsiders, from colonial officials to modern occult writers, filled the gap with fantasy. You do not need any of it to love her as her devotees do; most Kali worship, in homes and temples, is open, simple puja with flowers, lamps and song.

sections.heading: Time, and the night
sections.body:
Her name ties her to time (kala), which brings everything to its end. To fear Kali is, in a sense, to fear time, death and change. Her devotees turn that around: if the Mother is time, then even death is in her hands, and the child held by her has nothing to fear.

That is why she is worshipped at night, and above all on the new moon, the darkest night of the month. Darkness, for her devotees, is not evil. It is the dark before creation, the night in which everything rests, the deep blue of the sky and sea that her dark skin is said to be. Ramakrishna is remembered as saying that she looks dark only from far away, like the water of the sea, which is clear in your hands.

knowAndDont.known: Kali as a tongue of fire in the Mundaka Upanishad, Kalaratri in the Mahabharata, her emergence as Chamunda and the defeat of Raktabija in the Devi Mahatmya (Markandeya Purana cantos 87–88, Pargiter’s translation), and her place as first of the ten Mahavidyas are documented.
knowAndDont.unknown: The dates and places of most Tantric texts on Kali are uncertain, and some, such as the Mahanirvana Tantra, may be fairly late. How the different fierce goddesses of early India became one Kali is reconstructed, not known. Sayings of Ramakrishna come to us through his disciples’ records.

lessons.inPractice: Read cantos 87 and 88 of Pargiter’s public-domain translation of the Markandeya Purana this week, sitting before her lamp. You are reading to learn, not performing the Chandi Path; formal recitation is done in Sanskrit with its own rules, and is learned from a teacher. Write down one line each day that stays with you.
reflect: Kali is the Goddess’s own power sent out to do what nothing else could. What in your life needed fierceness to be done?
How do you feel about darkness: as something to fear, or as a time of rest before beginning?
further: F. E. Pargiter, trans., The Markandeya Purana (Calcutta, 1904; public domain), cantos 87–88
David Kinsley, Tantric Visions of the Divine Feminine: The Ten Mahāvidyās (1997)

lessons.title: Ramprasad, Ramakrishna and the Mother’s Children
lessons.summary: The Shakta poets of Bengal, the saint of Dakshineswar, and the songs still sung to her.

sections.heading: Ramprasad Sen
sections.body:
Ramprasad Sen (about 1718 to the 1770s) is the poet who, more than anyone, made Kali the tender Mother of Bengal. Born near Halisahar, north of Kolkata, he is said to have worked as a clerk and filled his ledgers with songs to Kali, until his employer, instead of dismissing him, gave him an allowance to sing. His songs, in plain Bengali, are still sung in homes, temples and on the radio, as Shyama Sangeet, "songs to the dark one".

He speaks to Kali as a child to its mother: complaining, teasing, pleading, scolding her for her neglect, and trusting her completely. In one song he tells his own mind that it does not know how to farm, and is letting the rich field of a human life lie fallow, when it could be growing gold by calling on her. In another he says that because she loves the cremation ground, he has made his heart a cremation ground, so that she will come and dance there.

sections.heading: Kamalakanta and the singers
sections.body:
After Ramprasad came many others. Kamalakanta Bhattacharya (about 1769 to 1821), court poet at Burdwan, wrote songs of great sweetness to the Mother and to Uma, the daughter who comes home at Durga Puja. Bengali Shakta poetry holds the two together: the cosmic Mother Kali, and the beloved girl Uma whose mother cannot bear to let her go.

In the twentieth century, Kazi Nazrul Islam, the great Bengali poet and himself a Muslim, wrote many Shyama Sangeet that are still sung. Singers such as Pannalal Bhattacharya made these songs loved across Bengal. Listening to them is one of the best ways to understand how Kali's devotees actually feel about her.

sections.heading: Ramakrishna at Dakshineswar
sections.body:
In 1855 Rani Rasmani, a wealthy widow of Kolkata, founded a temple to Kali on the Hooghly river at Dakshineswar, where the goddess is Bhavatarini. Its priest from 1856 was a young man from a village family, Gadadhar Chattopadhyay, known to the world as Ramakrishna (1836–1886). He longed so desperately to see the Mother that he wept at her feet, and he is remembered as having seen her as a boundless ocean of light. For the rest of his life he spoke of her as his Mother and himself as her child.

Ramakrishna taught that God could be reached by many paths, and that the Mother was present in every woman; he worshipped his wife, Sarada Devi, as the Goddess, and she is revered as the Holy Mother. His disciple Swami Vivekananda (1863–1902) brought his teaching to the West and founded the Ramakrishna Mission. Vivekananda's poem "Kali the Mother" (1898) says that the Mother comes to the one who dares to love even misery and death.

sections.heading: What the saints teach
sections.body:
The Shakta poets and saints teach something simple and hard: that the Mother's fierceness is for her children's sake. Ramprasad complains to her, and trusts her. Ramakrishna is frightened by nothing because he is her child. Their devotion is not about power, or about becoming fierce oneself, but about the trust of a child who knows its mother will not abandon it.

It is also joyful. Shyama Sangeet is full of humour and longing. Kali Puja is a festival of lamps and music. A devotee can laugh with the Mother, argue with her, and weep for her, and all of it is worship.

knowAndDont.known: Ramprasad Sen and his songs, Kamalakanta Bhattacharya, Nazrul Islam’s Shyama Sangeet, the founding of Dakshineswar by Rani Rasmani in 1855, Ramakrishna’s life there, Sarada Devi, and Vivekananda’s poem "Kali the Mother" are documented.
knowAndDont.unknown: Ramprasad’s exact dates and the stories of his life, such as the ledger of songs, are traditional and partly legend; some songs attributed to him may be by others. Ramakrishna’s sayings come through his disciples’ records, chiefly the Bengali Kathamrita by Mahendranath Gupta.

lessons.inPractice: Listen to Shyama Sangeet this week: songs of Ramprasad or Nazrul Islam, sung by artists such as Pannalal Bhattacharya, and read a few of Ramprasad’s songs in a good translation. If you can, visit a Ramakrishna Mission or Vedanta Society centre; many keep Kali Puja and welcome visitors.
reflect: Ramprasad scolded the Mother and trusted her completely. Can you speak to God, or to life, with that kind of honesty?
What would it mean to be afraid of nothing because you are someone’s child?
further: Leonard Nathan and Clinton Seely, trans., Grace and Mercy in Her Wild Hair: Selected Poems to the Mother Goddess by Rāmprasād Sen (1982)
Rachel Fell McDermott, Mother of My Heart, Daughter of My Dreams: Kālī and Umā in the Devotional Poetry of Bengal (2001)
Swami Vivekananda, "Kali the Mother" (1898; public domain), in his Complete Works

lessons.title: Kalighat, Dakshineswar and Kali Puja
lessons.summary: Her great temples, the new-moon night of Kali Puja, and her worship across India and beyond.

sections.heading: Her temples
sections.body:
Kalighat in south Kolkata is one of the most famous temples of the Goddess, counted among the Shakti Pithas, the places where parts of the body of Sati fell; here, the toes of her right foot. Its image of Kali, with large eyes and a long golden tongue, is unlike any other, and the city's name is often linked with it. Dakshineswar, across the city on the Hooghly, is Ramakrishna's temple, with twelve Shiva shrines along the river.

Beyond Bengal, she is Kalikamata on the hill of Pavagadh in Gujarat and Kalkaji in Delhi; she is honoured at Ujjain, and in Nepal at Dakshinkali near Kathmandu. In Kerala, Bhadrakali is worshipped in many temples, and Mudiyettu, a ritual dance-drama of her battle with the demon Darika, is recognised by UNESCO. Kali temples in the Caribbean, in Guyana and Trinidad, and among Tamil communities from Malaysia to South Africa, keep their own living traditions.

sections.heading: Kali Puja
sections.body:
Kali Puja, also called Shyama Puja, falls on the new moon of Kartika (by the reckoning that counts months from full moon to full moon), in October or November: the same night that much of India keeps as Diwali with Lakshmi Puja. In Bengal, Assam and Odisha the night belongs to Kali. Clay images are made and worshipped in homes, temples and huge neighbourhood pandals. The worship goes on through the night, with red hibiscus, lamps, sweets, mantras recited by priests and songs, and the city is lit with lamps and fireworks.

The night before is Bhoot Chaturdashi. Bengali families light fourteen lamps for fourteen generations of ancestors and eat fourteen kinds of leafy greens (choddo shaak). After Kali Puja, as with Durga, the images are immersed in water.

sections.heading: Her other nights
sections.body:
Every Amavasya, new-moon night, is hers, and many temples hold special worship. Tuesdays and Saturdays are also kept for her in many places. Phalaharini Kali Puja falls on the new moon of Jyeshtha, in May or June; it is especially kept at Dakshineswar, because on that night in 1872 Ramakrishna worshipped Sarada Devi as the Goddess. Ratanti Kali Puja falls in the month of Magha.

At Kalighat and Dakshineswar the daily worship begins before dawn, and on ordinary days crowds come with garlands of hibiscus, sweets and their worries, to speak to the Mother and go home lighter.

sections.heading: Gentle on the water
sections.body:
As with Durga and Ganesha, the clay images of Kali Puja are immersed after the festival. Images made with Plaster of Paris and chemical paints pollute rivers and lakes, and many communities now use natural clay and paints, or immerse in tanks made for the purpose.

If you keep a small clay image for Kali Puja, immerse it at home in a bucket of water, and pour the water and clay onto your garden when it has dissolved. A framed print, which is not immersed, is entirely traditional for a home shrine.

knowAndDont.known: Kalighat as a Shakti Pitha, the founding of Dakshineswar, Kali Puja on the Kartika new moon in eastern India, Bhoot Chaturdashi’s fourteen lamps and greens, Phalaharini Kali Puja and Ramakrishna’s worship of Sarada Devi in 1872, Kerala’s Bhadrakali worship and Mudiyettu (UNESCO, 2010), and Kali temples in the diaspora are documented.
knowAndDont.unknown: The age of Kalighat and of its image is not certain, and the link between the temple and Kolkata’s name is traditional. Kali Puja as a great public festival is often said to have grown in the eighteenth century under Raja Krishnachandra of Nadia, and its earlier history is debated.

lessons.inPractice: Find out when the next Kali Puja and Amavasya fall, using a Bengali panchang, the app’s Hindu calendar or a temple website. If you live near a Bengali community, look for a Kali Puja you can visit: dress respectfully, remove your shoes where others do, and accept prasad with your right hand. Many Kali Pujas run late into the night; a visit in the evening is enough.
reflect: On the darkest night of the year, Bengal lights lamps for Kali. What does it mean to you to light a lamp in the dark?
Bengali families remember fourteen generations of ancestors the night before. Whose names would you remember?
further: Rachel Fell McDermott, Revelry, Rivalry, and Longing for the Goddesses of Bengal (2011)
Sarah Caldwell, Oh Terrifying Mother: Sexuality, Violence and Worship of the Goddess Kāḷi (1999), on Bhadrakali in Kerala

practices.title: Lamp and red flower each day
practices.instructions: Each day, wash, remove old flowers, light the diya and offer one fresh red flower and a cup of water. Sit for a minute and say "Ma" before you study.
practices.prompt: One line: what did you learn about her today?

stages.title: Seven Nights to the New Moon
stages.intro: For seven nights, ending on Amavasya, the new moon, you will offer a simple puja each evening and sit with one aspect of the Mother, listening to a song of her devotees. If you can, keep these nights ending on Kali Puja itself; otherwise end on any new moon. First read the lesson on honouring her at home.

lessons.title: Honouring Her at Home Today
lessons.summary: Her offerings, her days, words and mantras, customs of respect, and the sensitive points.

sections.heading: Red hibiscus and sweets
sections.body:
Kali's flower is the red hibiscus, jaba in Bengali, offered singly or in garlands of 108; red is her colour, and red cloth and a little sindoor are offered too. Bel (bilva) leaves, sacred to Shiva, are used in her worship as well. Ghee or mustard-oil lamps, sandalwood and incense are traditional.

Her food offerings at home are simple and sweet: Bengali sweets such as sandesh and rasgulla, fruit, khichuri (rice and lentils), and luchi with vegetables. All offerings in this journey are vegetarian and offered untasted. Her devotees also offer songs: a Shyama Sangeet sung or listened to with love is as much an offering as a flower.

sections.heading: Her days
sections.body:
Amavasya, the new moon, is her night each month, and Kali Puja on the Kartika new moon is her great night of the year. Many devotees also keep Tuesdays and Saturdays for her, visiting the temple or offering a lamp and hibiscus at home.

She is called on in fear and danger, in illness and grief, at the end of things, and at the beginning of courage. Many Bengali families say "Ma" or "Jai Ma" before a journey, a hard task or an exam, as others say Ganesha's name.

sections.heading: Words and mantras
sections.body:
Hindus pray to Kali in their own words, in Shyama Sangeet and bhajans, in stotras (hymns) such as the Karpuradi Stotra and the lists of her names, and with mantras. The hymns of the Devi Mahatmya are public scripture, sung in temples and homes. Her Tantric mantras, though, are given only by a guru at initiation, with instruction about how and when to say them. They are not given here, and books or websites that offer them freely are not how her devotees learn.

You can pray freely in your own language and say her names: Ma, Kali, Shyama, Bhavatarini, Adya Shakti. If you want to recite in Sanskrit or sing in Bengali, ask a priest, teacher or Bengali friend; most will be glad you asked.

sections.heading: Customs of respect, and sensitive points
sections.body:
Remove your shoes. Offer with the right hand or both hands, food untasted and flowers unsmelled. Keep meat, eggs, alcohol and tobacco away from the shrine. Keep her image raised, clean and out of bathrooms. Do not use it on clothes, posters or tattoos as a design.

The most sensitive points with Kali are two. First, the Western "dark goddess": Kali is often taken as a symbol of rage, revenge or sexual power, or invoked in curses, in ways that her devotees find deeply hurtful. Second, Tantric practice: some books and teachers outside any lineage sell "Kali Tantra" rites. Real Tantric worship is given by a guru within a tradition, and imitating it is both disrespectful and unwise. Above all, go to a temple or a Kali Puja, and learn from people.

knowAndDont.known: Red hibiscus, red cloth, bel leaves, lamps and sweets as her offerings, Amavasya, Tuesday and Saturday devotion, Kali Puja, the Karpuradi Stotra and Shyama Sangeet, and the reservation of Tantric mantras to initiation are widespread in living practice.
knowAndDont.unknown: There is no single correct home puja; customs differ by family, region and sampradaya. Views on animal offering, and on fish in household offerings, differ and are debated within Hinduism.

lessons.inPractice: Find red hibiscus at an Indian grocer or flower market, or use red roses. Gather a few Shyama Sangeet recordings to listen to, one for each night. Choose the new moon that will be your seventh night, and clear the evening.
reflect: Which of the customs of respect is hardest for you, and why?
Where have you seen her image used carelessly or as a “dark goddess”, and how did it feel to notice it now?
further: David R. Kinsley, The Sword and the Flute: Kālī and Kṛṣṇa, Dark Visions of the Terrible and the Sublime in Hindu Mythology (1975)
Diana L. Eck, Darśan: Seeing the Divine Image in India (1981)

practices.title: Seven nights to the new moon
practices.instructions:
Each evening: bathe or wash, remove old flowers, ring the bell, light the diya and incense, and offer water, a red flower and a small sweet. Listen to or sing one Shyama Sangeet, or read one of Ramprasad's songs in translation. Then sit with the night's theme for ten minutes, wave the lamp three times clockwise before her image, bow, and take the prasad.

Night 1, Ma: the Mother and her child; what you would say to her if you trusted her completely. Night 2, Kala, time: what you are afraid of losing. Night 3, the sword: what ignorance or self-deception you would like cut away. Night 4, the garland: the words you speak, and the pride you wear. Night 5, the hands that bless: "do not fear", and the gift she holds out. Night 6, Shiva beneath her: stillness and power, and where you need each.

Night 7, Amavasya: offer a fuller puja with several red flowers, a sweet and two lamps. Sit in the dark with only the lamp burning, for as long as is safe and kind to your body, and listen to her songs. Before you sleep, say "Ma" once more.
practices.prompt: What did tonight’s aspect of the Mother show you about your fear, or your trust?

stages.title: After the New Moon
stages.intro: Take a few days with only the daily lamp and flower. Reread your journal. A vow of devotion is one good outcome; so is pausing, learning more at a temple first, or finding that your path lies elsewhere. A child who comes back to its mother later is still her child.

practices.title: Read your journal back
practices.instructions: Read your journal from the first flower. Note what drew you, what surprised you, and what you learned from people rather than from screens. Then answer the questions below.
practices.prompt: What has this month taught you about Kali, and about fear?

questions: Are you drawn to Kali herself, as Hindus worship her, as Mother, or to an idea of a "dark goddess" of rage, power or revenge? Be honest; only the first is what this vow is for.
Can you keep a small, clean daily practice (lamp, flower, a word to her) and the customs of respect through an ordinary year?
Have you visited a temple or a Kali Puja, or spoken with Hindu devotees? If not, would it be better to do that before any vow?
Would learning from a Hindu teacher or community, in time, serve your devotion better than a self-made vow? A vow now does not stop you doing that later.
If you decide to wait, or stop, can you offer her a last flower with thanks? That is a good ending too.

stages.title: A Vow of Devotion
stages.intro: If you choose to go on, this is a personal vow of devotion to Kali, made in a simple puja. It is not dīkṣā, not an initiation into any Hindu or Tantric tradition or lineage, and does not replace one; it does not make you a member of a sampradaya or give you anything a guru gives. It is your own promise of bhakti, as her child. An Amavasya, a Tuesday or Kali Puja itself are fitting days.

rite.title: Vow of Devotion to Kali
rite.summary: A full home puja in the evening with red hibiscus, lamps and sweets, honouring Ganesha first, your own vow (sankalpa) of devotion, a song to the Mother, arati and the sharing of prasad.

ingredients.name: Kali’s image, cleaned and garlanded if you can
A fresh red cloth for the shrine
A diya with ghee or mustard oil and a cotton wick, on a heatproof plate
A plate for the arati lamp
Red hibiscus flowers, or red roses, or a small red garland
Sandalwood paste or a little sandalwood oil
Bengali sweets or another vegetarian sweet, and fruit
A recording or the words of a Shyama Sangeet
Your vow, written on clean paper

rite.preparation:
During the day, write your vow. Keep it honest and keepable: what you will do (a daily lamp and flower, her new moons, a temple visit, Kali Puja each year, listening to her songs), what fear or pride you ask her to help you let go of, for how long (a year is common), and what you ask of her. Many people include a promise of service, such as caring for someone who is ill or afraid.

Bathe, dress in clean clothes (red if you like), and remove your shoes. Clean the shrine and lay the fresh red cloth. Prepare the food without tasting it.

steps.title: Begin with Ganesha
steps.instructions: At dusk, sit before her. Join your palms and breathe. Ring the bell. Honour Ganesha first with a flower and a bow.
steps.spoken: Ganesha, remover of obstacles, I bow to you first.

steps.title: Light and fragrance
steps.instructions: Light the diya and the incense. Touch a little sandalwood paste to the base of her image or its frame.

steps.title: Flowers and names
steps.instructions: Offer the red flowers one at a time, saying one of her names with each.
steps.spoken: Ma. Kali. Shyama. Bhavatarini. Adya Shakti. Dakshina Kali. Kalika…

steps.title: Food and water
steps.instructions: Set the sweets and fruit before her, with the cup of water. Sprinkle a few drops of water around the food.
steps.spoken: This food is yours, Ma. Accept it, and let it come back to us as your grace.

steps.title: The vow
steps.instructions: Take a little water in your right palm. Read your vow aloud, slowly. Let the water fall onto the plate beneath her, as a sign that the intention is made. Place the paper at her feet.

steps.title: Give her your fear
steps.instructions: Name honestly the fears you carry. Offer them to her, as a child hands its mother something too heavy to hold.
steps.spoken:
Ma, you who hold the sword and say "do not fear",
I am your child.
Take what I cannot carry,
and keep me close.

steps.title: A song
steps.instructions: Sing, or listen to, a Shyama Sangeet, with your eyes on her face.

steps.title: Arati
steps.instructions: Light the arati lamp from the diya. Wave it slowly in clockwise circles before her, from her feet to her face, while you sing or hum. Then pass your hands over the flame and touch them to your eyes and the top of your head.

steps.title: Sit with her
steps.instructions: Sit in silence before her in the lamplight.

steps.title: Close and share prasad
steps.instructions: Bow fully, or with joined palms. Take a sweet as prasad and share the rest with others today. Let the lamp burn while you are present, then cover it gently.
steps.spoken: Jai Ma. Thank you, Mother. I am your child, and I will keep my word.

rite.closing: Keep your vow folded near her shrine and read it each Kali Puja. Share the prasad. Return the flowers to the earth. Write the date in your journal. If you can, visit a Kali temple or a Ramakrishna centre in the coming weeks, and offer a red flower there.
rite.safety: Keep the diya, arati lamp and incense on heatproof plates, away from cloth, garlands, hair and loose sleeves, and never leave them unattended. If you use camphor for arati, burn only a small piece on a metal plate, keep it from children and pets, and never eat it. Keep sweets with chocolate, raisins or xylitol away from dogs and cats.

stages.title: The Mother’s Nights
stages.intro: After the vow, devotion is daily and yearly: a lamp and flower, her new moons, Kali Puja, her songs, temple visits, and a yearly renewal of your vow.

practices.title: Daily lamp and flower
practices.instructions: Each morning or evening, wash, light the lamp, offer a red flower and water, and say "Ma".

practices.title: Each new moon
practices.instructions: On each Amavasya (check a panchang), offer a fuller puja in the evening with red flowers and a sweet, listen to or sing a Shyama Sangeet, and sit with her lamp in the dark for a while. Give something to someone who is struggling.
practices.prompt: What has the Mother carried you through this month?

practices.title: Kali Puja
practices.instructions: Each year on the Kartika new moon, in October or November, keep Kali Puja. On the night before, Bhoot Chaturdashi, light fourteen small lamps for your ancestors. On the night itself, offer red hibiscus, lamps and sweets, sing or listen to her songs, and visit a temple or community Kali Puja if you can. If you keep a small clay image, immerse it at home afterwards and give the water to your garden.
practices.prompt: What did the night of Kali Puja, and the people you kept it with, show you this year?

practices.title: Yearly renewal
practices.instructions: On the anniversary of your vow, or at Kali Puja, reread it, write it anew, and repeat the vow puja. Change it honestly. If you are ending it, offer a last red flower and sweet with thanks, take down the shrine with care, and give the image to a temple or immerse a clay image respectfully.
practices.prompt: What has a year as the Mother’s child changed in you?
